title: Beyond caste names
hook: Singh and Kaur were meant to replace caste surnames

segments.voice: Yesterday, craftsmen and builders: Ramgarhia Sikhs, and the honest bread of Lalo the carpenter. Your line was builders.

A form on a screen. First name. Last name. The second box is doing more work than it looks. In a lot of places, a last name quietly tells a stranger where your family comes from, what your great-grandparents did for a living, sometimes which well they were allowed to drink from. This week has met Sikh communities known by a trade, a region, a history. A question sits under all of them: what happens to the second box when a Guru hands everyone the same name?
screen: `FIRST NAME. LAST NAME.` → `WHAT A SURNAME TELLS A STRANGER.` → `THE SAME NAME FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Begin at Anandpur, a story this path has told before. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh called for heads, the five who stood up came from different families and trades, and after the Amrit each was given the same name: Singh for the men, Kaur for the women who took Amrit. In a world where a surname announced your caste, one shared name meant nobody could read your birth off it. Second, the root under the name. Long before Anandpur, Guru Nanak had chosen a side. In a line from the opening pages of the Granth, in paraphrase, he keeps company with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to keep up with the great. Where the lowly are cared for, there the gaze of grace falls. A shared name is that line turned into a habit. Third, the honest part. Names didn't stop at Singh and Kaur. Some Sikh families still carry a caste or clan name after them, and you've met communities this week who are still known by one. Some Sikhs drop the surname and go by Singh or Kaur alone. Some add a village. Some keep the family name for a passport and leave it off everywhere else. Sikhs argue about this among themselves, and the argument itself shows the old ideal is still alive. Last, a name is the first thing anyone learns about you. Two shared names make a stranger ask you something else first.
screen: `AT ANANDPUR, ONE NAME FOR FIVE.` · `NANAK STANDS WITH THE LOWEST.` · `SURNAMES CAME BACK, AND SIKHS ARGUE.` · `A STRANGER HAS TO ASK SOMETHING ELSE.` · then, large: `ONE NAME FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Say your own last name silently, and ask what it tells people before you've said a word: a country, a family, a religion, a class, a story. Some of that you may be proud of, and some you never chose; hold it gently, without judging. Then let the name go for a few breaths and just be the one breathing, resting on Waheguru if you pray.
Beyond caste names. Singh and Kaur, given to every Sikh who takes Amrit, so that a surname would no longer tell anyone a person's caste. Today's word.
Your line: one name for all. A name can open a door instead of closing one. See you tomorrow.
